title: Sustainable alternatives to petroleum-based micro/nanospheres: a systematic scoping review on biodegradable materials and applications
abstract: Abstract Adhering to PRISMA-ScR guidelines, this systematic review evaluates sustainable alternatives to petroleum-based micro/nanospheres. We classify biodegradable materials into natural, synthetic, and composite systems, analyzing their fabrication alongside diverse applications in cosmetics, biomaterials, environmental remediation, catalysis, and thermal energy storage. By addressing technical trade-offs, standardized testing, and critical research gaps, this work provides a strategic roadmap for engineering high-performance, eco-friendly microspheres to mitigate the global microplastic crisis and promote a circular bioeconomy.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Polymeric particles are typically classified as microspheres (or microparticles) ranging from 1 to 1000 μm and nanospheres (or nanoparticles) smaller than 1 μm 1 . In practice, microspheres are frequently referred to as “microbeads,” but this term can also encompass larger particles that reach the millimeter scale 2 , 3 . The small, spherical geometry of these particles provides a high surface-area-to-volume ratio that enables diverse applications 4 . Polymeric microbeads are used across multiple sectors as exfoliants in cosmetics, controlled-release carriers in agriculture, and adsorbents for environmental remediation, while serving as critical platforms for drug delivery, cell encapsulation, and diagnostics in biomedical fields. The most common and conventional materials for polymeric sphere production have been primarily petroleum-based plastics like polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), and polystyrene (PS) 5 , 6 . While these materials provide clear convenience and performance advantages in everyday products and industrial processes, their persistence after use has emerged as a significant environmental drawback, contributing to the accumulation of microplastics in aquatic and terrestrial environments. In particular, their small size enables them to escape capture during wastewater treatment, facilitating their release into receiving waters, subsequent accumulation in ecosystems, and potential bioaccumulation through the food chain, thereby posing risks to both environmental and human health 7 , 8 .

Accordingly, these environmental and potential human health risks have prompted regulatory measures worldwide to restrict plastic microbeads and, more broadly, to regulate intentionally added microplastics in consumer and industrial products. In response, a global regulatory movement has emerged to restrict fossil fuel based plastic microbeads, particularly those added to rinse-off personal care products. Initial policy interventions focused on preventing “down-the-drain” releases by limiting the manufacture, import, and sale or distribution of rinse-off cosmetics containing intentionally added plastic microbeads 9 , 10 . However, cosmetic focused restrictions address only a subset of added microplastics, and concerns persist regarding polymeric microparticles used in other consumer and industrial product categories. Consequently, regulatory attention has expanded from product specific bans toward broader frameworks that cover intentionally added microplastics across sectors. In particular, the EU REACH restriction introduced a cross sector approach by regulating synthetic polymer microparticles placed on the market on their own or intentionally added to mixtures, thereby accelerating the demand for sustainable alternatives 11 . This broader regulatory trend has reinforced the need to develop biodegradable polymeric micro and nanospheres that can meet performance requirements while minimizing environmental persistence. This escalating environmental concern and regulatory momentum have made the development and adoption of sustainable alternatives not just imperative, but urgent. Accordingly, research on biodegradable polymeric micro and nanospheres has expanded rapidly across academia and industry.

In this context, biodegradable polymer micro and nanospheres have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional nondegradable plastic microbeads, with expanding utility in cosmetics, biomedical, and environmental applications. Biodegradable micro and nanospheres are attracting attention because they can be engineered to deliver the functionality of conventional plastic microbeads while offering a post-use degradation pathway that reduces long term environmental persistence. Unlike fossil fuel-based microbeads that are designed to remain dimensionally and chemically stable during use and therefore tend to persist after release, biodegradable particles can be formulated to undergo hydrolytic, enzymatic, or microbial degradation depending on their chemistry, crystallinity, crosslinking density, and surface characteristics. Importantly, the same molecular and colloidal design freedom that enables performance tuning, such as controlled size distribution, porosity, and surface functionality, also provides levers to tune degradation kinetics and environmental fate. Consequently, the development of biodegradable microbeads is increasingly viewed not as a simple material substitution but as a materials design problem that integrates performance, safety, and degradability.

In this review, we provide an overview of recent advances in the design, properties, and applications of biodegradable polymeric spherical particles. We classify sustainable micro and nanospheres by material platform and hybridization strategy, encompassing natural and biomass-derived polymers, biodegradable synthetic polymers, and composite or hybrid particles incorporating inorganic or bioactive components. We also summarize fabrication approaches that enable control over particle architecture, including size distribution, morphology, porosity, and structural stability, which together determine performance in end-use conditions. Based on these design factors, we discuss how structure–chemistry relationships govern key functions in personal care, biomedical, and environmental applications, while also shaping degradation behavior and environmental fate. Accordingly, this review consolidates recent advances in biodegradable micro and nanospheres and outlines future research directions to accelerate their development and adoption as sustainable alternatives to conventional plastic microbeads.

sections.heading: Cosmetics and personal care products
paragraphs: Microbeads are widely utilized in cosmetics and personal care products for exfoliation, sensory enhancement, and controlled delivery of active ingredients. To perform these functions safely and effectively, microbeads must satisfy a set of physicochemical and biological performance criteria. Regarding their mechanical properties, microbeads must procure a balance between sufficient rigidity to facilitate exfoliation and enough malleability to avoid skin or tissue damage 12 . As these materials come into direct contact with human skin, their biocompatibility must be assessed through in vitro cytotoxicity assays and clinical tests such as skin patch studies, to ensure they do not induce adverse skin irritation and inflammation 13 . Additionally, growing concerns regarding microplastic pollution have underscored the need for microbeads to be biodegradable and environmentally benign 14 . The ability of microbeads to meet these functional and environmental requirements is primarily dictated by the chemical nature and structural characteristics of their constituent polymers. A comprehensive overview of these parameters, as analyzed in the studies included in this review, is provided in Table  1 . Natural and biomass-derived polymers are particularly attractive for microbead fabrication due to their inherent biodegradability and biocompatibility. Among them, alginate stands out for its unique advantages in personal care applications because it combines excellent skin compatibility with rapid environmental degradation. Its ability to form stable hydrogels under mild conditions also makes it easy to process into microbeads 15 . Bae et al. fabricated alginate microbeads using an electrospraying method for cosmetic applications 16 . This study demonstrated that alginate concentration and nozzle diameter correlated with the mass flow rate of the liquid, affecting the size and morphology of the microbeads. The alginate microbeads achieved complete degradation by day 28 via ion-exchange with seawater. Notably, this structural breakdown triggered the desorption of captured contaminants, posing a potential environmental hazard upon rinse-off. Additionally, material performance within cosmetic formulations remains to be fully characterized.

In addition, cellulose and its derivatives represent another major class of polysaccharide-based materials used in microbead fabrication, particularly valued for their structural robustness and surface modifiability 17 . Kim et al. developed cellulose microbeads using membrane emulsification with cellulose acetate as a precursor, achieving high processing efficiency 17 . As shown in Fig.  1a , fabricated cellulose microbeads exhibited a compressive strength of 5.72 MPa, comparable to that of commercial vinyl dimethicone beads (6.31 MPa), indicating their suitability for incorporation into cosmetic formulations. Furthermore, the beads exhibited no cytotoxicity and maintained high cell viability even at concentrations up to 1000 µg mL −1 . This study reveals that cellulose microbeads can match the physical performance of synthetic counterparts while maintaining biocompatibility, supporting their viability as safe functional ingredients in cosmetic formulations. Beyond their inherent biodegradability, novel green fabrication techniques enhance the sustainability of PHA microspheres 18 ,  19 – 20 . Choi et al. successfully employed a solvent-free melt-electrospraying process to produce uniform poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-4-hydroxybutyrate) (P3HB-4HB) microbeads (Fig.  1b ) 19 , whereas You et al. demonstrated a scalable solvent exchange method to fabricate poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate) (PHBV) using the eco-friendly solvent dimethyl isosorbide (DMI), aligning with green chemistry principles by eliminating toxic organic solvents often required for biopolymer processing 20 , 21 . Unlike the irregular surfaces of natural alternatives like walnut shells these PHA microbeads exhibit spherical morphologies and smooth surfaces that ensure safety while maintaining cleansing efficiency comparable to or exceeding commercial PE microbeads. These materials also address ecological concerns by showing lower adsorption of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) compared to PE and microcrystalline cellulose, reducing the risk of toxin transport in marine environments. PHBV microbeads exhibited excellent biocompatibility with no toxicity to plants or aquatic life (zebrafish) and demonstrated selective degradation, remaining stable during sterile storage while biodegrading effectively in marine conditions. Collectively, these findings suggest that PHA-based microbeads represent a comprehensive solution for next-generation personal care products, combining industrial scalability, superior performance, and environmental safety.

While biomass is inherently renewable, the conventional extraction of purified biopolymers often requires rigorous processing involving toxic solvents, which compromises its environmental benefits 22 , 23 . To address this, approaches focusing on direct utilization or minimal processing of biomassare being explored, including in the fabrication of polymeric micro/nanospheres 24 , 25 . McMackin et al. investigated a method to convert brewer’s spent grain (BSG), a major byproduct of the brewing industry, into functional microbeads 25 . The process involved dissolving acid-hydrolyzed BSG pulp directly into an aqueous NaOH/ZnO system at 50 °C. The mixture was then extruded into an acid coagulation bath to regenerate the polymeric structure, producing spherical microbeads. This process yielded beads with a porous internal structure and an indentation hardness of 199 MPa. This specific hardness and contaminant removal test proved its effectiveness as an exfoliating material, also gentler than many irregular natural abrasives. Although the process exhibits a high E-factor (about 130, reflecting waste intensity), the acidic processing solutions can be recycled, and the final microbeads are fully biodegradable. This offers a functional and sustainable alternative to both commercial microplastics and irregular natural exfoliating materials.

Overall, these studies demonstrate that biomass-derived and biopolymer-based microbeads can achieve cosmetic-grade performance, biocompatibility, and environmental safety; however, their broader adoption remains constrained by incomplete understanding of long-term stability in complex cosmetic formulations, trade-offs between structural durability and controlled environmental degradability, and the need to further optimize green processing routes to reduce waste intensity and ensure true life-cycle sustainability.

Beyond the intrinsic biodegradability of natural polymers, a parallel strategy focuses on engineering synthetic polymers, which allow for precisely controlled degradation pathways and tailored high-performance properties, such as mechanical stability, and consistent processability. For instance, Nam and Park demonstrated an eco-friendly approach by avoiding the use of organic solvent. In this study, they controlled the molecular weight of commercial PLA and PCL with electron-beam treatment to optimize them for a solvent-free melt electrospraying method (Fig.  1c ) 26 . These microbeads demonstrated effective cleansing performance comparable to commercial products. Notably, their lower specific surface area restricted the adsorption of POPs, effectively reducing the potential for toxic bioaccumulation compared to conventional porous microbeads.

However, under seawater conditions, the degradability of PLA and PCL microbeads presented limited progress compared to conventional non-degradable polymers. According to the study by Nam and Park, PLA and PCL microbeads showed negligible weight loss in natural seawater over 56 weeks, indicating high persistence, while degradation was significantly accelerated in alkaline solutions (pH 11) 26 . This indicates that while they are biodegradable under industrial composting conditions (high temperature and humidity), their degradation kinetics in natural marine environments remain insufficient for them to be considered a rapid solution for marine microplastic pollution, especially when compared to fully marine-degradable biopolymers such as PHAs.

Additionally, the study investigated skin hydration and trans-epidermal water loss (TEWL) as performance indicators. While the results effectively showed that PLA and PCL microbeads outperformed PE (polyethylene) and MCC (microcrystalline cellulose) in the TEWL assessment, no mechanistic explanation was provided for this superior performance.

In a different approach, poly(β-amino ester) (PAE) microbeads were developed by designing the polymers from the monomer level (Fig.  1d ) 27 . The polymer was engineered to undergo hydrolytic degradation, breaking down into small, environmentally benign molecules such as sugar and amino acid derivatives. When fabricated into smooth, spherical microbeads with an average diameter of approximately 76 µm, the PAE microbeads improved the removal of permanent marker stains by 2.4 times compared to soap alone. Beyond simple exfoliation, the microbeads also proved effective at contaminant removal, adsorbing 82% of copper from a solution. However, unlike PLA and PCL which have well-established production pathways, PAE constitutes a novel class of biodegradable polymers. Despite offering precise degradation control and generating benign byproducts 28 , PAE applications remain confined to laboratory-scale studies due to insufficient large-scale synthesis protocols and incomplete safety assessments 29 .

Taken together, these studies indicate that engineered synthetic polymer microbeads offer advantages in processability, mechanical stability, and controllable degradation behavior; however, their practical sustainability is limited by slow degradation kinetics in natural marine environments, incomplete mechanistic understanding of skin-performance benefits, and, in the case of emerging polymers like PAE, the absence of scalable manufacturing routes and comprehensive toxicological validation.

Polymeric microbeads composed of a single material can inherently suffer from various limitations, as it is difficult to simultaneously optimize mechanical stability, degradation behavior, and functional performance within a single polymer system. Consequently, composite strategies that combine multiple materials with complementary properties have been increasingly explored as a means to overcome these intrinsic constraints.

Composite microbeads enable the integration of diverse functionalities by rationally combining polymers with distinct physicochemical characteristics. Such approaches allow improvements in degradation kinetics, surface properties, and functional performance that are difficult to achieve when using single-component systems alone. Among biodegradable polyesters, poly(lactic acid) (PLA) has been widely investigated for microbead fabrication owing to its renewability, biocompatibility, and well-established processing routes. However, PLA-based microbeads typically exhibit slow degradation in aqueous environments and lack inherent functional activities, such as antioxidant properties. To overcome these limitations, Kim et al. introduced a composite fabrication strategy in which lignin was adsorbed onto the surface of PLA microbeads 30 . This polymer–polymer surface complexation approach produced multifunctional microbeads with markedly enhanced properties. Specifically, the lignin-adsorbed PLA microbeads exhibited a 163-fold increase in antioxidant activity compared to neat PLA microbeads. In addition, the hydrophilic nature of lignin accelerated hydrolytic degradation by approximately 1.3 times, effectively mitigating the persistence issues commonly associated with synthetic polyester microbeads in aquatic environments. This study demonstrates that composite strategies based on polymer–polymer surface interactions provide a promising route to simultaneously enhance the biodegradability and functional performance of PLA microbeads.

Although composite microbeads offer clear advantages in addressing the limitations of single-material systems, several challenges remain to be resolved. The selection of compatible material combinations, long-term stability of interfacial interactions, and reproducibility of composite structures can significantly influence performance outcomes. In addition, increased formulation complexity may introduce challenges related to scalability, cost, and regulatory compliance, particularly for cosmetic applications requiring consistent quality and safety. Despite composite strategies represent a promising direction for enhancing both the biodegradability and functionality of microbeads, further systematic studies are required to address remaining challenges in material compatibility, stability, scalability, and environmental impact, and to establish design principles.

Sunscreen is another category of personal care product in which polymeric spheres are incorporated as leave-on materials. In such formulations, polymer spheres serve as either UV filter carriers or function as UV-shielding agents themselves. In addition to the general physicochemical requirements outlined in the ‘exfoliants and bioactive carriers’ section, microbeads used in sunscreens must meet specific criteria related to photoprotection performance. Key requirements include high photostability, effective sun protection factor (SPF), the ability to scavenge reactive oxygen species (ROS), and minimizing the risk of skin penetration, particularly under UV exposure 12 . Studies investigating microparticles for UV protection have generally evaluated these criteria, the results of which are comparatively presented in Table  2 . These additional demands highlight the need for careful material selection and surface engineering of microbeads used in sunscreen formulations, especially when aiming for both efficacy and safety in long-term skin contact under sunlight. Alongside the fundamental need for functionality and biocompatibility, there is a growing imperative for sustainability and environmental protection in sunscreen formulations. Consequently, natural polymer-based microencapsulation, utilizing proteins and polysaccharides, has emerged as a promising solution 31 ,  32 ,  33 – 34 . While many polysaccharides possess semi-crystalline structures, starch offers a distinct advantage due to its unique granular morphology. Native starch granules exhibit a radial, onion-like structure composed of alternating crystalline and amorphous lamellae 35 . This specific architecture facilitates controlled enzymolysis, wherein enzymes selectively hydrolyze the susceptible amorphous regions while preserving the overall granular integrity 36 , 37 . Harnessing this property, Zhang et al. encapsulated UV filters within enzymatically hydrolyzed porous corn starch granules, employing whey protein as an outer sealant 37 . This dual-layer design utilized the enhanced porosity of the modified starch to maximize UV filter loading, while the protein shell effectively prevented leakage and contributed to UV attenuation through light scattering. Consequently, this dual layer increased the SPF value and photostability compared to the unencapsulated sunscreen (SPF increased by 62.24%). Crucially, the design drastically minimized skin permeation, ensuring that the UV filters remain effective on the skin surface rather than penetrating into skin tissues, thereby resolving a major safety concern associated with organic filters.

Another strategy for developing sustainable and biosafe sunscreens involves utilizing the intrinsic properties of natural polymers themselves. Lignin is a prime candidate due to its natural UV-shielding ability, yet its dark color has been a major barrier to its use in cosmetics 38 , 39 . To overcome this challenge, Zhang et al. developed light-colored microspheres by treating bamboo lignin with acetic acid. This acted as chemical modification to reduce chromophores and physical restructuring into microspheres to decrease bulk density, successfully mitigated the inherent color issue (Fig.  2a ) 38 . Consequently, this formulation achieved high UV protection efficacy (SPF 56.8 at 5% w/w) without visible skin discoloration, demonstrating that lignin can be rationally modified to meet the esthetic standards of commercial cosmetics while retaining its functional efficacy. Silk fibroin also functions as a natural UV-protective material. Its aromatic residues enable UV absorption and ROS scavenging, while its β-sheet structure imparts high photostability 40 , 41 . Wang et al. developed silk fibroin microspheres (SFMPs) that exhibited superior photostability compared to conventional organic sunscreens (OMC) and antioxidant capabilities exceeding those of inorganic TiO 2  (Fig.  2b ) 42 . This performance was attributed to the ethanol-induced self-assembly process, which increased the β-sheet content for stability, and the optimized particle size maximized UV reflectance, facilitating antioxidant activity. Moreover, in vivo and ex vivo studies further indicated that SFMPs form a stable barrier on the skin without penetrating deeper layers, suggesting their potential as safe and effective sunscreen materials.

Collectively, these studies highlight the growing potential of natural polymer-based microencapsulation for the development of sustainable and biosafe sunscreen formulations. From a critical perspective, the practical translation of natural polymer-based sunscreen microbeads remains subject to several challenges. Variability in raw material sources, batch-to-batch reproducibility, and sensitivity to processing conditions can significantly influence particle structure and performance. In addition, achieving consistent optical properties, long-term stability in complex cosmetic formulations, and scalability at an industrial level remains nontrivial. Regulatory considerations, particularly regarding purity, allergenicity, and long-term skin exposure, must also be carefully addressed. Therefore, while natural polymer-based microencapsulation represents a highly promising route toward next-generation sustainable sunscreens, further systematic studies are required to establish standardized design principles that balance functional performance, esthetic requirements, manufacturing feasibility, and regulatory compliance.

Synthetic biodegradable polymers allow precise control over particle properties, such as morphology, size distribution, and amphiphilic balance. While amphiphilic balance is critical for stabilizing lipophilic UV filters, morphology and size significantly enhance the intrinsic light-scattering effect of the polymeric microspheres 43 , 44 . Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), a water-soluble and biocompatible polymer, has been used to encapsulate the triazine UV filter, bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine (BEMT) 45 . In this study, PVA formed stable shells for controlled release and enabled safer aqueous manufacturing compared with solvent-intensive methods. Encapsulation addressed the key drawbacks of free BEMT, including strong lipid solubility and risks of allergy or leaching. PVA–BEMT microcapsules with a uniform core-shell structure were prepared through emulsification, solvent removal, and spray drying. The resulting capsules exhibited improved dispersion, reduced leakage, and enhanced UV absorption. Optimized formulations achieved SPF values of about 57 and PFA values of about 25 when added to creams, exceeding the performance of pristine BEMT and maintaining stronger photoprotection under accelerated aging tests.

Polyphosphazenes provide a versatile platform for photoprotection due to their unique P=N backbone that combines inorganic and organic features. This chain structure enables tunable degradability, high biocompatibility, and broad functionalization capabilities 46 . Recently, Zhou et al. developed self-framed microparticles via copolymerizing hexachlorocyclotriphosphazene with quercetin, a flavonoid that provides both UV absorption and antioxidant activity (Fig.  2c ) 47 . This approach effectively addressed the inherent limitations of quercetin—namely, low solubility, rapid photodegradation, and skin permeability—while integrating UV filtering with potent ROS scavenging. The resulting particles exhibited high quercetin loading, broadband UVA and UVB absorption with SPF values exceeding 36. Also, they demonstrated excellent photostability, retaining over 93% of UV shielding efficiency after 8 hours of irradiation. The covalently crosslinked architecture prevented small molecule leakage and dermal penetration, and in vivo assays confirmed significant protection against UV-induced DNA damage.

These recent studies highlight the potential of synthetic biodegradable polymers as versatile platforms for sunscreen microencapsulation. Nevertheless, several practical challenges remain for their implementation in commercial sunscreen formulations. The long-term degradation behavior of synthetic polymer matrices, including the identity and safety of degradation byproducts under prolonged UV exposure, remains insufficiently understood. From a regulatory perspective, synthetic materials may also be subject to more stringent evaluation than naturally derived polymers, particularly with respect to chronic skin exposure and potential environmental accumulation. Therefore, while synthetic biodegradable polymers represent a promising strategy for advanced sunscreen microbead design, further efforts are required to simplify fabrication routes, establish comprehensive degradation and safety profiles, and align material development with regulatory and life-cycle considerations to facilitate practical implementation.

Although synthetic aliphatic polymers are explored as a biodegradable sunscreen formulation, limitations such as acidic degradation byproducts, solvent residues, and hydrophobicity persist. On the other hand, relying solely on natural polymers often compromises structural stability and scalability due to swelling. To bridge this gap, incorporating robust and tunable inorganic or biocompatible polyester materials with natural polymers has emerged as a viable solution 48 ,  49 – 50 . In this context, Choi et al. developed a plastic-free encapsulation platform comprising chitosan-coated mesoporous silica particles (mSOCPs) to impregnate octyl methoxycinnamate (OMC) (Fig.  2d ) 51 .

The mesoporous silica core provided a mechanically stable, non-swelling framework that facilitated high UV filter loading, overcoming the structural vulnerabilities of pure polymeric carriers. Moreover, the intrinsic tendency of mesoporous silica towards premature leakage was effectively mitigated by the chitosan shell. This biopolymer coating served a dual function: physically blocking the silica pores to suppress OMC leakage and actively scavenging ROS through its intrinsic antioxidant activity. As a result, the encapsulated OMC exhibited substantially enhanced photostability (~20% degradation after 3 h, compared to ~80% for free OMC) and achieved approximately 99% suppression of ROS generation. Despite these advantages, hybrid inorganic–biopolymer systems may introduce additional complexity in interfacial design and raise concerns regarding long-term colloidal stability and process scalability, which should be carefully addressed for practical cosmetic applications.

sections.heading: Biomedical and pharmaceutical applications
paragraphs: Moving beyond their conventional role as passive carriers, recent progress aims to design “smart”, stimuli-responsive polymeric spheres that dynamically interact with physiological environments 52 . Unlike traditional ceramics or glass-based substrates, polymeric matrices offer tunable biodegradability and high surface-area-to-volume ratios, enabling high therapeutic loading with minimized long-term persistence in the body 53 ,  54 – 55 . Natural polymers, including polysaccharides (e.g., alginate, chitosan) and proteins (e.g., silk fibroin, zein), are premier candidates for biomedical scaffolds due to their inherent biocompatibility and abundance of functional groups for modification 56 . Protein-based microspheres have been extensively investigated for their amphiphilic nature and the presence of specific amino acid sequences that promote cell adhesion or conjugation with bioactives and biodegradation via enzymatic pathways 57 ,  58 – 59 . Among these various nature derived biopolymers, carboxymethylated chitosan (CMCS) is an advantageous prodrug material due to its solubility at neutral physiological pH, biodegradability, and low toxicity 60 ,  61 – 62 . Its chemical structure provides abundant amine groups that serve as grafting points for drug-linker conjugates, while its carboxyl groups provide both solubility and a mechanism for pH-responsiveness. A key strategy for enhancing therapeutic efficacy involves designing stimulus-responsive systems from these materials. For example, dual-responsive nanoparticles were fabricated by conjugating 10-hydroxycamptothecin (10-HCPT) onto CMCS via a pH- and enzyme-sensitive succinyl linker 63 . When dispersed in aqueous solution, this polymer self-assembles into spherical structure, resulting in CMCS segments to form the outer shell while 10-HCPT becomes a core due to its hydrophobicity. Under simulated tumor conditions (pH 5.0 with enzyme), these formulations showed a 4.6-fold increased drug release over 12 hours compared to physiological pH (7.4) and exhibited cytotoxicity 4.5 times higher against 4T1 cancer cells than the free drug. The pH-responsive mechanism involves the protonation of the CMCS carboxyl groups under acidic conditions, which causes the particle to swell into a loosened nanogel matrix. This structural change facilitates enzyme penetration, accelerating the cleavage of the ester bond and triggering site-specific drug release.

Beyond stimulus-responsive drug delivery, microspheres can be fabricated into active functional scaffolds for in situ tissue regeneration by recruiting endogenous stem cells and then inducing them to differentiate into targeted cells. To demonstrate this, porous chitosan microspheres were fabricated and implemented as a template due to their biocompatibility and mucoadhesive properties (Fig.  3a ) 64 . Porous chitosan microspheres were developed using high-voltage electrostatic spraying with liquid nitrogen collection, followed by freeze-drying. This method created a porous architecture that enhanced Bone Morphogenetic Protein-2 (BMP-2) loading by nearly 50% and enabled more prolonged release profile compared to nonporous spheres. To achieve targeted stem cell recruitment, the microbeads were functionalized with a CD271 antibody, resulting in highly selective recruitment of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), with 85.9% of captured cells being CD271-positive. By simultaneously driving differentiation and regeneration, the system achieved significantly enhanced bone repair in a rat femoral defect model, outperforming all control groups. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that a chitosan microbead platform can effectively drive CD271-mediated stem cell recruitment and BMP-2-induced differentiation, facilitated by its high porosity and abundant conjugation sites, thereby enabling effective in situ tissue repair without the need for ex vivo cell manipulation. While natural polymers excel in bio-interfacing, they often suffer from batch-to-batch variability. Biodegradable synthetic polymers (e.g., PLA, PLGA, PVA) address this limitation by offering precise control over molecular weight and degradation kinetics. Although their synthesis often involves organic solvents, the high degree of control over polymer architecture (e.g., molecular weight and monomer ratios) allows for the precise engineering of particle size and degradation kinetics, which are essential for ensuring predictable and sustained drug release profiles 65 ,  66 ,  67 – 68 . PLA and PLGA are widely favored for their low immunogenicity, which prevents premature clearance associated with antibody generation 69 .

Among biodegradable synthetic polymers, poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA) is widely utilized for its excellent biocompatibility and FDA approval 70 , 71 . As in the form of microspheres fabricated by emulsification and solvent evaporation method, the relationships between their size and drug loading and release kinetics have been explored 72 . Smaller PLGA microspheres (<20 μm) were found to release drugs rapidly via diffusion, whereas larger particles (>50 μm) exhibited sustained release governed by erosion. Lower loading in smaller particles was attributed to their higher surface-to-volume ratio, facilitating greater drug loss during fabrication, while the faster release observed in larger microspheres was due to the autocatalytic effect of acidic byproducts trapped within their core. These findings underscore that particle size and drug delivery kinetics analysis are crucial steps for achieving predictable drug release. PLGA was also introduced as a versatile polymeric carrier for prodrug delivery in treating complex inflammatory conditions such as acute lung injury (ALI) 73 . It is biocompatible and offers sustained drug release and effective loading of hydrophobic drugs such as curcumin. In this system PLGA was hybridized with PEG matrix and surface modified with sialic acid to achieve precision at both tissue and subcellular levels were developed. Furthermore, curcumin was modified with cations that facilitate mitochondria targeting (Fig.  3b ). Tissue-level specificity is achieved through surface functionalization with sialic acid (SA), which selectively binds E-selectin, a receptor upregulated on inflamed pulmonary vascular endothelium during ALI. For subcellular precision, the microspheres encapsulating Cur-TPP actively target mitochondria, the primary site of oxidative damage.

Poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) is utilized as a versatile synthetic platform, primarily due to its dense hydroxyl groups and excellent gel-forming capability, making it a promising template for biocatalysts 74 ,  75 – 76 . Piacentini et al. found that enzyme immobilization method is critical for performance; specifically, entrapment via membrane emulsification yielded a superior enzymatic activity recovery of 78%, drastically outperforming adsorption or post cross-linking of the enzyme on the PVA matrix (<10%) 67 . This enhanced efficiency arises from the interfacial activation of lipase during the water-in-oil (W/O) emulsification process, where the enzyme spontaneously migrates to the interface and is locked in its active conformation.

However, similar to chitosan-based systems, a critical sustainability challenge persists regarding the chemical cross-linking step required to stabilize the water-soluble PVA matrix. This stabilization process conventionally relies on glutaraldehyde, a reagent well-known for its cytotoxicity and environmental hazards 77 ,  78 – 79 . Although glutaraldehyde effectively solidifies the matrix via acetal linkage formation, its application compromises the green profile of the final product. Consequently, current research is increasingly adopting greener strategies, including physical cryogelation or the use of non-toxic, bio-based cross-linkers such as genipin and citric acid 80 ,  81 ,  82 – 83 . However, transitioning to these alternatives introduces new trade-offs regarding mechanical integrity and cost. Therefore, future efforts must focus on optimizing these green fabrication routes to achieve the structural robustness required to rival conventional glutaraldehyde-based systems.

Chemical cross-linking within a single polymer matrix, or composite systems have been adopted in the pursuit of enhanced structural robustness and functional performance 84 ,  85 ,  86 – 87 . While alginate hydrogels are premier biomaterials, their high swelling ratio often precludes the sustained release required for prolonged therapies like wound healing. Shi et al. addressed this challenge by incorporating CaCO₃ as an inorganic filler to modulate the hydrogel network 88 . Crucially, the authors demonstrated that the drug release profile could be precisely tuned by adjusting the inorganic filler content. Increasing the CaCO₃ concentration restricted polymer chain mobility, thereby suppressing the burst effect and prolonging release duration. The low-filler matrix was utilized for the rapid release of rifamycin to adress initial inflammation, while the high-filler matrix ensured the sustained release of bFGF for tissue repair. By combining these tailored populations, the system achieved a staged therapeutic effect enabling sequential wound management.

Moreover, to achieve on-demand delivery, alginate hydrogels were hybridized with iron oxide nanoparticles to create injectable macroporous ferrogels. A critical fabrication challenge can occur during the pore-forming step. While EDTA was necessary to remove the CaCO₃ template, it inadvertently stripped the structural Ca²⁺ crosslinks, causing the matrix to collapse. To circumvent this instability, a sequential cross-linking strategy was applied 89 . By introducing a permanent covalent network following initial ionic stabilization, the authors successfully engineered a robust matrix capable of withstanding template removal. This resilient macroporous architecture not only significantly enhanced protein loading capacity but also enabled precise mechanical actuation. Upon magnetic stimulation, the matrix underwent volumetric deformation, generating internal convection that triggered a rapid, on-demand burst release.

To overcome the limited bioavailability and instability of labile compounds like astaxanthin (AST), a hierarchical ‘liposome-in-microsphere’ composite was developed, integrating molecular targeting with physical protection (Fig.  3c ) 90 . Specifically, Human Serum Albumin (HSA)-modified liposomes were encapsulated within an alginate/hydroxymethyl chitosan hydrogel shell. This composite architecture served a dual function: the outer polymeric shell provided a pH-responsive barrier against gastric degradation and enhanced mucoadhesion, while the inner HSA-liposomes facilitated receptor-mediated intestinal absorption. This synergistic design significantly minimized nutrient loss during transit and enhanced bioavailability, effectively preventing hypercholesterolemia in vivo compared to non-encapsulated controls.

While these composite and hierarchical systems clearly demonstrate how rational material integration can impart sustained, staged, or on-demand release functionalities that are difficult to achieve with single-component matrices, their increased structural and compositional complexity also introduces new challenges. Precise control over filler distribution, interfacial stability between distinct components, and batch-to-batch reproducibility becomes increasingly demanding as system hierarchy increases. In addition, scalable manufacturing and regulatory evaluation may be complicated by multicomponent architectures, particularly for clinical or pharmaceutical translation. Therefore, future efforts should focus not only on expanding functional sophistication but also on establishing simplified design rules that balance performance, manufacturability, and translational feasibility.

Spherical particles dominate diagnostic platform design because their high surface-area-to-volume ratio maximizes the immobilization of biorecognition molecules, enhancing assay sensitivity. Their uniform geometry also ensures predictable fluid dynamics and reproducible kinetics. While platforms based on traditional materials like polystyrene and gold nanoparticles have been foundational 91 , they possess inherent limitations such as poor biodegradability, high manufacturing costs, and reliance on fossil-fuel-driven matrices. Given that most diagnostic consumables are single-use, the accumulation of non-biodegradable biomedical waste has become a critical environmental concern 92 . These drawbacks have driven contemporary research toward advanced materials, particularly natural polymers, biodegradable synthetic polymers, and their composites 54 . Table  4  provides an overview of the detection methods, target molecules, and techniques used across different systems for biosensing and diagnostic applications. This section traces these polymer-based platforms, highlighting how biodegradable materials can meet the rising demand for rapid, sensitive, and eco-conscious diagnostics. Natural polymers are attractive materials for biosensing and diagnostics owing to their renewable availability and abundance of reactive functional groups. However, their inherent polydispersity and susceptibility to degradation under harsh environmental conditions constrain practical utility 93 . Strategic green fabrication process can address these challenges by enhancing structural stability while maintaining environmental benignity. Particularly in immunoaffinity chromatography, the stationary phase requires high ligand density and uniform packing 94 . To meet these criteria, chitosan microbeads were fabricated via membrane emulsification, which is also a low-energy technique that generates uniform droplets under mild conditions, unlike energy intensive high shear dispersion methods (Fig.  4a ) 93 , 95 . The resulting monodispersity facilitates consistent column packing and reproducible flow characteristics, thereby maximizing the separation efficiency of the chromatographic system. Subsequent chemical cross-linking conferred pH stability across a broad range, while comparative analysis demonstrated that the resulting chitosan microbeads exhibited zearalenone (ZEN) extraction efficiency and reproducibility equivalent to the commercial agarose matrix (Sepharose 4B). Furthermore, with their fine-tuned elasticity, hydrogel microspheres can be applied to mechanical phenotyping 96 . In this approach, microbeads serve as physical references to classify cells based on differences in their mechanical properties, such as elasticity and deformability, thereby simplifying the diagnostic process. For example, alginate hydrogel beads themselves were utilized in a label-free cancer diagnostic method (Fig.  4b ) 97 . By tuning the cross-linking density, the elasticity of the beads was adjusted to serve as a physical cutoff in microfluidic channels, distinguishing softer cancer cells from harder normal cells with >95% accuracy. This approach not only uses biodegradable materials and eliminates the use of hazardous chemical labels but also converts a complex biophysical measurement into a simple, relative comparison.

However, the exclusive use of natural polymers is limited by their batch-to-batch variability and structural instability in complex fluids despite their superior bio-interfacing capabilities. Conversely, synthetic biodegradable polymers such as PLA and PLGA offer excellent reproducibility and mechanical stability, yet their inherent chemical inertness and hydrophobicity hinder efficient antibody conjugation 71 , 98 . Crucially, neither material class possesses intrinsic signal transduction capabilities, such as magnetism for separation or fluorescence for detection. To overcome these dual limitations regarding surface chemistry and passive functionality, the field has converged on a composite strategy. This approach hybridizes stable polymer matrices with functional inorganic or organic reporters to enable high-performance and multiplexed diagnostics 99 .

The integration of magnetic nanoparticles into polymer matrices facilitates magnetic separation or acts as nucleation templates to regulate particle morphology. From a sustainability standpoint, magnetic responsiveness offers clear advantages. It allows the diagnostic platform to be easily recovered and reused, reducing biomedical waste and simplifying the workflow. Replacing complex centrifugation or filtration steps with straightforward magnetic isolation also minimizes both operational time and energy consumption 100 , 101 .

In the study of Wu et al., multicompartmental alginate hydrogel microspheres containing specific functional cargo, such as fluorescent nanoparticles and magnetic beads, were fabricated using 3D microfluidic droplet generation 102 . This system utilizes axisymmetrically arranged channels to form patterned laminar flows upstream, which are subsequently exposed to downstream shear stress to create monodisperse droplets with multicompartmental layouts. These droplets are then solidified through acid-triggered internal cross-linking (via Ca-EDTA) to preserve their distinct compartmentalized structures. In this system, magnetic nanobeads are conjugated with miRNA detection probes; this not only ensures the stable immobilization of the probes within the hydrogel matrix but also facilitates the ease of separation and purification during microsphere fabrication. Within each particle, compartments contain specific identifiers (fluorescent polystyrene nanoparticles) or capture probes (magnetic bead-DNA complexes), allowing for the simultaneous detection of multiple miRNA targets. This 3D microfluidic approach demonstrated high monodispersity and detection sensitivity. Furthermore, the successful generation of super-segmented particles with up to 20 compartments represents a significant advancement in high-throughput multiplexed biosensing.

Additionally, these magnetic nanoparticles can induce heterogeneous nucleation by providing specific sites for polymer assembly, thereby guiding the formation of uniform structures 103 , 104 . For instance, in the study by Luo et al., starch-based composite microspheres were fabricated for bacterial sensing 105 . Specifically, enzymatic debranching of waxy maize starch was conducted to produce short-chain glucans to address the inherent polydispersity of starch polymers. Then, dextran-coated iron oxide nanoparticles (Dex@IONPs) were introduced to seed and guide the uniform self-assembly of these glucans, creating size-controlled magnetic beads for efficient separation. This approach achieved a bacterial capture efficiency of over 90% and demonstrated excellent functional stability over three recycling cycles.

Another study also utilized a magnetic dextran matrix yet focusing on fluorescent optical multiplexed assays 106 . They implemented a facile process for optical barcoding that circumvents the complex, multi-step fabrication required by traditional encoding methods. Uniform dextran microbeads were first prepared with membrane emulsification. Subsequently, a layer of dendrimers was coated onto the beads via electrostatic adsorption, creating an exceptionally dense layer of amine functional groups critical for high-density antibody attachment. Optical fluorescent barcodes were then generated in a single step by reacting this surface with a mixture of fluorescent and non-fluorescent NHS ester linkers (Fig.  4c ). By simply varying the linker ratio, a library of beads with distinct fluorescence intensities was created for multiplexed assays. As a result, the platform achieved an antibody immobilization density approximately 50-fold higher than conventional methods. This high immobilization density enabled a highly sensitive 3-plex cytokine assay with limits of detection in the low pg/mL range (2–3.9 pg/mL).

Quantum dots (QDs) have emerged as powerful optical reporters for multiplexed biosensing due to their size-tunable and narrow emission spectra, along with exceptional resistance to photobleaching 107 , 108 . Although their inorganic nature and constituent heavy metals (e.g., Cd, Se) present limitations regarding biodegradability and potential toxicity, their optical superiority over conventional organic dyes makes them indispensable for high-performance in vitro diagnostics 109 . To harness these optical benefits while ensuring biocompatibility in detecting bioactive substances, encapsulating within biodegradable polymer matrices can serve as a safety strategy 110 ,  111 ,  112 – 113 .

Accordingly, an ultrasensitive multiplexed platform utilizing polylactic acid (PLA) microspheres encoded with CdSe/ZnS QDs was developed 114 . The PLA matrix provided a biocompatible barrier, yet its inherent chemical inertness posed a challenge for antibody attachment. To resolve this limitation, maleic anhydride (MA) was grafted onto the microspheres to create carboxyl-rich surfaces and support strong bioconjugation. Produced with SPG membrane emulsification, these “PLA-MA” microspheres successfully encapsulated the QDs, generating 9 distinct spectral barcodes. This hybrid approach effectively combined the multiplexing ability of inorganic QDs with the functional versatility of organic biopolymers. This enabled the simultaneous quantification of four tumor markers with high sensitivity. In addition, encapsulating QDs can help mitigate the potential toxicity risks associated with heavy metal leakage 115 ,  116 – 117 .

Furthermore, the simultaneous encapsulation of magnetic nanoparticles and QDs often leads to fluorescence quenching, which hampers detection performance 118 . To address this, Lan et al. utilized a flow-focusing microfluidic strategy to fabricate alginate-based Janus microparticles, which spatially isolate Fe 3 O 4  and QDs into distinct hemispheres 119 . The study emphasized that the physical properties of these particles are highly tunable through key experimental parameters, including flow rate, viscosity matching, and diffusion prevention to maintain the stability of the diphasic laminar flow interface. The practical functionality was validated through a model DNA assay, demonstrating clear signal discrimination between target and non-target samples. Such precise control over particle morphology and composition under mild conditions, which avoids harsh UV or thermal treatments, highlights the potential of biopolymer Janus particles for diverse biomedical and sensing applications.

Additionally, polydopamine (PDA) has become a versatile and biocompatible platform in biosensing due to its ability to self-polymerize under mild conditions and its abundant surface functional groups that enable diverse conjugations. Recent advances highlight PDA’s potential to serve not only as a surface modifier but also as an active sensing component. Zhang et al. exemplified this by designing aptamer-functionalized PDA nanospheres that simultaneously isolate and detect small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) within a single system (Fig.  4d ) 120 . The Fe³⁺-doped PDA core enabled rapid colorimetric readout through Prussian blue formation, providing a simple and instrument-free assay with sensitivity exceeding that of conventional ELISA. This study demonstrates the evolving role of PDA-based composites as integrative biosensing platforms. By unifying separation and detection steps while eliminating the need for complex instrumentation, this approach offers a low toxicity and energy-efficient solution.

Overall, polymeric microspheres have evolved from simple passive supports into sophisticated, multifunctional architectures essential for next-generation multiplexed diagnostics. The convergence of high-throughput multiplexing and the inherent biocompatibility of natural polymers opens new frontiers for both in vitro and potentially in vivo sensing. Furthermore, adopting sustainable matrices offers a practical solution to reduce the environmental impact of single-use biomedical waste. Continued advancements in structural engineering and material selection will lead to diagnostic tools that are both clinically effective and environmentally sustainable.

paragraphs: Environmental pollution from heavy metal ions, oils, and organic matter poses escalating threats to ecosystems, driving extensive research into sustainable remediation technologies. Among various removal methods, physical adsorption offers distinct advantages due to its simplicity, low cost, and energy efficiency 121 . In this context, bio-based polymeric microspheres have emerged as compelling candidates. Their abundant surface functional groups and hydrophilic nature facilitate strong interactions with aqueous contaminants. Furthermore, their biodegradability addresses the secondary pollution risks associated with synthetic adsorbents, making them a practical solution for sustainable wastewater treatment 122 ,  123 ,  124 ,  125 – 126 . The primary advantage of chitosan as an adsorbent matrix lies in its high density of reactive amine groups. These moieties function as active sites for pollutant binding, making chitosan a promising candidate for anionic pollutant removal 127 , 128 . This mechanism was effectively demonstrated by the successful removal of iodide anions, using cross-linked chitosan microspheres 125 . The study elucidated that the protonated amine groups (-NH 3 + ) were the core contributors to capturing anionic species (I - ) via electrostatic attraction. Significantly, the cross-linked chitosan microspheres maintained an adsorption efficiency of over 95% across a broad pH range (pH 4–10) and retained performance over five cycles. This demonstrates that bio-based materials like chitosan, when properly engineered for stability, can be comparable counterparts to synthetic polymeric adsorbents.

Although cellulose possesses advantages as a sustainable material, its intrinsic adsorption capacity for heavy metal ions is limited 129 . Consequently, surface modification strategies have been widely adopted to enhance its performance 130 ,  131 ,  132 ,  133 – 134 . For instance, employing the chelating affinity of phosphorous moieties, phosphate groups were introduced into the cellulose chain to target lead ions (Pb 2+ ) in water (Fig.  5a ) 135 . This modification not only introduced binding sites, but also increased porosity and specific surface area. The primary adsorption mechanism involves the deprotonation of the phosphate groups (-PO 3 H 2 ) into negatively charged sites (-PO 3 2- ), which then bind with cationic Pb 2+  through strong electrostatic interaction and chelation. The resulting phosphorylated cellulose microspheres exhibited a rapid equilibrium time (within 30 minutes) and a high maximum adsorption capacity (108.5 mg/g), demonstrating the efficacy of chemical functionalization. While these studies clearly demonstrate that bio-based polymers such as chitosan and cellulose can be engineered into highly effective adsorbent microspheres through crosslinking and chemical functionalization, several practical considerations remain. The adsorption performance of amine- or phosphate-functionalized biopolymers is often strongly dependent on solution pH, ionic strength, and the presence of competing ions, which may limit their effectiveness in complex real-world water matrices. In addition, repeated adsorption–desorption cycles can induce structural fatigue or the gradual loss of functional groups, potentially compromising long-term reusability. Consequently, while functionalized biopolymer adsorbents show competitive performance compared to synthetic counterparts under controlled conditions, further studies are required to evaluate their durability, regeneration efficiency, and robustness under realistic environmental conditions.

Biodegradable aliphatic polyesters, such as PLA and PLGA, possess inherent advantages in targeting non-polar pollutants due to their hydrophobic backbones. The presence of methyl groups renders these materials oleophilic, facilitating strong hydrophobic interactions with oils and organic solvents 136 , 137 . Capitalizing on these properties, nanoporous poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) microspheres were developed as rapid toluene and oil adsorbents via thermally induced phase separation (TIPS) technique (Fig.  5b ) 138 . This study revealed that the non-solvent content governed the phase-separation mechanism, while the good solvent controlled the nucleation and microsphere size. The resulting spherulitic microspheres exhibited superhydrophobic and oleophilic properties, enabling the rapid and selective removal of toluene and oil from surfactant-stabilized emulsions.

Despite these functional advantages, the reliance on biodegradable synthetic polymers derived from first-generation (edible) biomass has sparked debate, calling into question whether they constitute an authentically sustainable, closed-loop resource. To address this sustainability dilemma, studies exploring polymers synthesized from second-generation (non-edible) biomass as precursors are being conducted 139 ,  140 – 141 . In this context, furfuryl methacrylate (derived from agricultural byproduct furfural) was copolymerized with maleic anhydride to create high-performance adsorbent 142 . Subsequent surface modification with amine or carboxyl groups established a clear structure-function relationship. The amine groups enhanced electrostatic attraction toward anionic dyes, while the carboxyl groups, once deprotonated, facilitated better adsorption by Pb²⁺ coordination through both electrostatic and chelation effects. This approach exemplifies how bio-derived synthetic polymers can bridge the gap between waste valorization and functional material design.

Compostie microspheres targeting environmental remediation are also evolving into intelligent, multifunctional systems 143 . By integrating capabilities such as stimuli-responsive desorption, antifouling coatings, and in-situ catalytic degradation, these advanced materials are now capable of autonomous or semi-autonomous environmental remediation, enabling not just pollutant capture but also self-regeneration and destruction 99 , 144 . As an example of fouling-resistant design, chitosan microspheres featuring a magnetic core and silver nanoparticles (AgNP) surface coating were developed (Fig.  5c ) 145 . The chitosan shell facilitates adsorption and the magnetic core enables rapid separation. Additionally, AgNPs serve a dual purpose by imparting strong antimicrobial and antifouling properties and preventing the formation of bacterial biofilms that typically clog pores and reduce efficiency in real-world wastewater. Analysis confirmed that while untreated beads were compromised by a thick biofilm, the silver-decorated composites completely inhibited bacterial growth, ensuring long-term performance.

Recently, novel processing techniques are being developed to faciliate the fabrication of highly tunable composites. A scalable production of porous graphene/alginate microspheres was achieved by integrating a 3D-printed inkjet nozzle with a gas-liquid microfluidics 146 . Beyond the improved production rate (800 µL/min), the integration of sodium alginate enhanced adsorption performance. The alginate introduced negatively charged, oxygen-containing functional groups onto the graphene surface. This created strong electrostatic attraction for positively charged dyes (e.g., methylene blue) while simultaneously repelling negatively charged compounds. This study highlights how composite microspheres can be successfully produced with the combination of scalable process with precise chemical selectivity for targeted remediation.

Based on these applications, future critical challenges will involve ensuring scalable and economical production processes for these advanced materials. Furthermore, their stability and selectivity must be validated in complex matrices representative of real-world wastewater. By assigning distinct functional roles within a single particle, these multifunctional composites can optimize the balance between remediation efficiency and environmental sustainability. Validating such designs in real-world applications through quantitative studies will be essential to facilitate the transition from laboratory research to feasible practical applications in environmental remediation.

In addition to the filtration and adsorption functions of materials, recent applications demand the rapid and precise sensing of pollutants or toxic substances. In this domain, spherical platforms offer distinct structural advantages. Their high surface-area-to-volume ratio amplifies interactions with target analytes 147 , 148 , while their uniform geometry ensures signal reproducibility 149 ,  150 – 151 . Complementing these physical attributes, recent research has pivoted toward the design of sensors that are bio-inspired, eco-friendly/biodegradable, or integrated with multi-stimuli hybrid systems 152 , 153 . With the rising demand for eco-friendly material and the excellent hygroscopic property of silk fibroin (SF), a silk fibroin humidity sensor as in Whispering Gallery Mode (WGM) resonator was investigated 154 . WGM sensors trap light through total internal reflection, generating an exceptionally sharp resonant peak at a specific wavelength. This resonance exhibits high sensitivity to minute changes in both the resonator size and surface refractive index 155 . As humidity increases, water absorption induces volumetric expansion of the sphere, causing a proportional redshift in the resonant wavelength. Crucially, the flexible random coil regions absorb moisture and allow for the volume change, while the rigid β-sheet structures provide the mechanical stiffness to maintain the sphere’s morphology. This ensures high stability and reversible sensing for the WGM resonator.

Upon exposure to nitrite, the beads undergo a Griess reaction, producing a visible azo dye for smartphone-based colorimetric quantification. Furthermore, the dense calcium-crosslinked network functioned as a size-exclusion filter, allowing small target ions to permeate while blocking interfering macromolecules like proteins, thereby enabling direct analysis of complex food matrices. Resolving the high cost and instability of purified biomolecules, whole-cell microbial biosensors have emerged as a robust alternative 157 , 158 . Lee et al. engineered a field-deployable sensor by encapsulating genetically modified bacteria within alginate-cellulose microbeads (Fig.  6b) 159 . Their bioreporters, designed to fluoresce in the presence of nitroaromatic explosives such as TNT or DNT, were co-encapsulated with nitro-binding M13 phages for enrichment of the local analyte concentration. Of note, the reinforcement of the alginate matrix with carboxymethyl cellulose increased mechanical strength and provided an advantageous microenvironment due to its biocompatibility, resulting in prolonged bacterial activity. The resulting system achieved nanomolar detection limits with remote optical readout capabilities. Despite the inherent viability constraints of microbial sensors, this study illustrates that structural reinforcement of the matrix can effectively prolong biological activity. This highlights the potential of engineered whole-bio-based systems as specific and sensitive alternatives to conventional chemical probes.

While these examples demonstrate the versatility of natural polymer-based microbeads as platforms for physical, chemical, and biological sensing, several challenges remain for their broader deployment. Sensor performance based on hygroscopic swelling, chemical colorimetric reactions, or biological activity can be highly sensitive to environmental conditions such as temperature, pH, and matrix composition, potentially affecting signal stability and reproducibility. In addition, long-term operational stability, particularly for systems relying on biomolecules or living cells, remains a key concern due to gradual degradation, leaching, or loss of biological activity. Integration into portable or wearable devices may also require further optimization of mechanical robustness, signal calibration, and standardization. Therefore, although natural polymer-based sensing microbeads offer compelling advantages in terms of sustainability, specificity, and multifunctionality, continued efforts are needed to improve robustness, lifetime, and real-world reliability for practical sensing applications.

In composite systems, synthetic biodegradable polymers are often employed to enhance the structural stability of the hydrogel-based sensors. Li et al. developed a sensor using alginate hydrogel microsphere cross-linked with a hyperbranched synthetic biodegradable polymer 160 . The hydrogel matrix combines hyperbranched poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (HB-PEGDA) and thiolated alginate (SA-SH). Specifically, SA-SH provides hydrophilicity, while multi-armed HB-PEGDA serves as a robust 3D crosslinker. Critically, the rapid thiol-Michael addition reaction enabled the stable co-encapsulation of dual fluorescent probes (for Al³⁺ and Hg²⁺) without leakage. However, the sensor becomes unstable below pH 6 due to probe hydrolysis, which limits its application in acidic environments like acid mine drainage, thus requiring further chemical optimization 161 , 162 .

On the other hand, algal biomass can be converted into functional sensors, representing another method of sustainable micro/nanoparticle design. Targeting the toxic cyanobacteria byproduct, microcystin-LR, cellulose/inorganic rattle-type microspheres were hydrothermally fabricated from  Chlorella pyrenoidosa  (Fig.  6c ) 163 . In this one-pot hydrothermal process, the intrinsic cellulosic cell wall of the algae acted as a robust microreactor and shell template, while the internal protoplast served as a carbon source. The resulting composite featured a mesoporous cellulose shell for antibody conjugation and a magnetic inorganic core for separation. When applied in an ELISA format, these microspheres achieved a detection limit for microcystin-LR ten times lower than conventional assays. This study demonstrates how biomass-derived materials can be transformed into multifunctional microspheres that combine structural tunability, magnetic manipulability, and bio-interfacing capability for pollutant detection in environmental monitoring.

Collectively, biodegradable polymer-based sensor platforms are evolving from passive encapsulation matrices into active functional systems capable of signal amplification and intrinsic responsiveness. As demonstrated by the optical resonance of silk fibroin and the analyte enrichment in phage-integrated microbeads, the field is shifting toward maximizing active sensing capabilities. However, future research must address the inherent instability of natural polymers in extreme environmental conditions through advanced hybridization strategies. Ultimately, the convergence of active optical structures, robust hybrid composites, and remote interrogation techniques will define the next generation of sustainable environmental monitoring tools.

While agrochemicals are indispensable for managing the escalating abiotic and biotic stresses on crops, their intensive use has precipitated multifaceted environmental crises. Excessive fertilizer use leads to nutrient runoff and eutrophication, while petroleum-derived polymeric additives contribute to microplastic contamination 164 , 165 . Additionally, widespread pesticide application further raises concerns about non-target toxicity, bioaccumulation, and ecological disruption 166 . These issues necessitate the development of environmentally benign delivery technologies that preserve agrochemical efficacy while minimizing ecological harm. Consequently, achieving controlled release and phyto-compatibility has become a central focus in sustainable agricultural research. Zein, a hydrophobic corn protein, is often limited by poor aqueous dispersibility. Hao et al. addressed this limitation by chemically modifying zein into an amphiphilic nanocarrier 174 . Their core strategy involved a ring-opening reaction using ethylene glycol diglycidyl ether (EGDE) as a linker to graft a hydrophilic carboxymethyl cellulose copolymer (CMC-g-P(HEMA-MMA)) onto the zein backbone (Fig.  7b ). This amphiphilic transformation not only improved dispersibility but also enhanced pesticide encapsulation efficiency compared to simpler modifications. Particularly, the functional CMC shell provided multifunctional protection. It enhanced anti-UV properties through physical shielding and improved adhesion to plant foliage. Furthermore, the system exhibited pH-responsive release behavior, enabling environment-specific delivery that minimizes off-target leaching.

Overall, natural polymers offer biodegradable platforms, but their release behavior is often passive and diffusion-controlled, and it is heavily dependent on the soil environment 175 . Conversely, synthetic biodegradable polymers such as PLA and PLGA often require specific industrial composting conditions to degrade completely. Consequently, they exhibit poor biodegradability in natural soil conditions, posing a higher risk of persisting as agricultural microplastics. To overcome this passive limitation and to achieve both precise control and sustainability, a dominant strategy is hybridization with stimuli-responsive materials to create externally tunable release systems.

Stimulus-responsive delivery systems represent a critical advancement in precision agriculture. By reacting to external triggers-pH, temperature, or light-these systems minimize the required dosage of agrochemicals. Wang et al. developed a photoresponsive composite platform via surface-grafted cinnamamide functionalized with γ-cyclodextrin (γ-CD) (Fig.  7c ) 176 . UV exposure triggered the photoisomerization of cinnamamide, disrupting the inclusion complex and releasing herbicide. The platform released more than 80% of the encapsulated content under light exposure but less than 15% in the dark. This on-demand mechanism significantly reduces environmental loss during the dark, when plant growth and herbicidal activity are less active. Despite its effectiveness, the practical applicability of light-triggered delivery systems may be constrained by variable light availability and penetration under field conditions, necessitating further validation in realistic agricultural environments.

Current efforts are geared towards resolving these issues with multi-responsive systems within a single matrix. Yang et al. developed a dual-stimuli responsive soil conditioner with temperature and pH-triggered release mechanisms. The system utilized a biodegradable chitosan matrix functionalized with a poly(N-isopropylacrylamide-co-methacrylic acid) [P(NIPAM-co-MAA)] copolymer, which conferred temperature sensitivity via the NIPAM component (LCST ≈ 32 °C) and pH responsiveness through the MAA component (Fig.  7d ) 177 . In acidic conditions, rapid liberation of the alkaline fertilizer (urea) neutralized soil pH to promote plant growth, while at temperatures above the LCST, PNIPAM contraction expelled water and nutrients to mitigate heat stress. Although PNIPAM is biocompatible, it is a non-biodegradable synthetic polymer. This presents a sustainability paradox within the context of biodegradable materials. However, we highlight this study because the ecological benefits regarding the significant reduction in fertilizer runoff and enhanced crop resilience offer a compelling trade-off against the persistence of the material. Future iterations must aim to replace these synthetic switching units with fully biodegradable analogs to achieve a completely closed-loop lifecycle.

Alginate–silica hybrid microbeads were developed for hydrometallurgical applications, particularly in the recovery of REEs 182 . Specifically, neodymium (Nd) was chosen as a representative model element for the group of critical REEs, as it exhibits a high coordination affinity with alginate’s carboxylic acid groups 187 . Using vibrating-nozzle technology, alginate suspensions were shaped into monodisperse microspheres via calcium-induced ionotropic gelation. Silica was incorporated either by in situ polymerization of tetramethyl orthosilicate (TMOS) or by the direct addition of silica powders (Fig.  8a ). Both routes yielded hybrid structures with markedly improved stability compared to pristine biopolymer beads, but the method of silica introduction strongly influenced adsorption performance. The TMOS-derived interpenetrating networks generate rigid frameworks with high specific surface area; however, the reduced fraction of alginate within the matrix resulted in fewer carboxylate binding sites and lower adsorption capacity. By contrast, composites formed with silica powder (M600) achieved greater absolute adsorption capacity due to a higher density of organic binding sites, despite their low surface area and structural refinement. Beyond technical efficiency and highly productive fabrication method demonstrated in this study, the recovery of Nd from industrial residues is crucial for establishing a sustainable supply chain for green technologies. As Nd is an indispensable component for high-strength permanent magnets utilized in advanced electronics and clean energy systems, this recovery approach provides an alternative to traditional mining, which is often environmentally taxing and faces supply-chain challenges 188 , 189 .
