Natural polymer–MOF hybrids have emerged as efficient adsorbents for the selective recovery of Heavy Rare Earth Elements (HREEs). Imidazolate-based MOFs are promising due to their nitrogen-rich linkers, abundant metal coordination sites, and hierarchical porosity that facilitates multivalent ion capture. However, their instability and poor retrievability in acidic aqueous environments limit large-scale deployment. Recent studies have shown that embedding these MOFs within natural polymer matrices, such as cellulose acetate or alginate hydrogels, significantly improves structural stability. Functioning as a protective shield, the polymer matrix mitigates metal leaching and preserves the MOF structure even under wastewater conditions (Fig.  8b ) 183 , 184 . This hybridization strategy bridges the gap between high-performance synthetic sorbents and environmentally sustainable materials, positioning imidazolate MOF–polymer composites as scalable candidates for green REE recovery.

Moreover, gold (Au) recovery from E-waste was demonstrated with the development of eco-friendly chitosan-based microspheres that employ an adsorption-reduction cascade mechanism (Fig.  8c ) 185 . In this approach, chitosan was functionalized with ferrocene to introduce redox activity, and crosslinked with oxidized cyclodextrin to improve stability. Additionally, thiourea was incorporated to provide sulfur-containing binding sites for selective gold capture. The composite is fabricated into porous microbeads through freeze-thaw cycles and freeze-drying, creating a hierarchical porous structure that enhances surface area and accessibility for gold ions. Of note, the practical viability of this system was validated using real e-waste streams. The results confirmed that the combination of hierarchical porosity and specific surface chemistry enabled high recovery rates even in dilute solutions.

sections.heading: Catalysts and energy materials
paragraphs: Spherical architectures, especially those characterized by high porosity, provide a significant specific surface area and an increased density of accessible active sites, both of which are paramount for efficient catalytic reactions and rapid electron transfer. Such structural attributes directly facilitate improvements in volumetric energy density and rate performance within both energy storage and catalytic frameworks. This section prioritizes the discussion on spherical biopolymer matrices hybridized with catalytic or energy-storing species, emphasizing systems where the polymeric integrity is maintained throughout the functionalization process. A primary benefit of these platforms is the avoidance of high-temperature calcination. By bypassing such harsh thermal treatments, these polymeric matrices preserve abundant functional groups that promote effective coordination with diverse guest materials. Furthermore, these mild processing environments allow for the seamless integration of labile bioactive species, such as enzymes and proteins, which would otherwise be denatured under the extreme conditions required for carbonization. Accordingly, the thermochemical conversion of biomass into carbonaceous microspheres is considered beyond the scope of this review due to the fundamental shift in material properties and the loss of the native polymeric characteristics that occurs during calcination. The following subsections investigate recent progress in natural polymer-derived materials specifically tailored for catalytic applications and energy storage systems.

Catalysts are essential materials that enhance energy efficiency by reducing the activation energy required for chemical reactions and contributing to sustainability by minimizing undesirable byproducts. Metals such as platinum (Pt) and palladium (Pd) are frequently employed as catalysts due to their superior redox properties; in biological contexts, biomolecules or enzymes are similarly utilized. However, these catalytic agents often suffer from agglomeration, which leads to a loss of functionality, and their small size makes them difficult to retrieve after reactions. To address these challenges, hybridizing catalysts with stable, spherical matrices enables uniform distribution on the support surface, thereby enhancing catalytic efficiency and facilitating recovery. Among the various sustainable candidates, lignin-derived materials have emerged as particularly promising supports due to their chemical robustness and abundance 190 ,  191 ,  192 – 193 . Recent studies have explored their versatility in applications ranging from environmental remediation to energy production. For instance, Shen et al. developed Pd nanoparticles supported on lignin nanospheres via a tandem fractionation and dialysis process, achieving outstanding efficiency in the reduction of toxic Cr(VI) to Cr(III) under solar irradiation 194 . Beyond environmental applications, these lignin-based carriers have also shown great potential in fuel synthesis. Additionally, Pang et al. demonstrated this by fabricating lignin microspheres (LMS) as palladium (Pd) nanoparticle carriers via a surfactant-assisted hydrothermal method, avoiding the use of toxic organic solvents 195 . In this system, the LMS functioned as both a catalyst carrier and a green reducer, where the abundant phenolic hydroxyl groups of lignin facilitated the reduction of Pd 2+  ions into Pd 0  nanoparticles. These LMS-supported Pd catalysts achieved efficient hydrogen generation from formic acid decomposition, outperforming unsupported Pd nanoparticles and offering reusability after multiple reaction cycles (Fig.  9a ). While these lignin-based systems effectively manage chemical reductions, the complexity of specific environments, such as groundwater, often requires more sophisticated architectural designs to maintain stability. To address this, amphiphilic Janus nanoparticles doped with Zero Valent Iron (ZVI) as catalysts were developed using the electrohydrodynamic co-jetting technique 196 . Hemispheric particles were fabricated by simultaneously passing two distinct polymer solutions through side-by-side needles under an electric field. This approach imparts an amphiphilic nature to the particles while providing protection to ZVI, a potent agent for in situ water remediation. Although ZVI is highly effective, its practical application is often hindered by rapid oxidation and severe agglomeration in aqueous systems. To overcome these challenges, ZVI was integrated into a specialized polymeric matrix for photo-responsive release. In the optimized architecture, ZVI nanoparticles were encapsulated in both compartments: one consisting of a hydrophobic PLA matrix, and the other a PLA/PE (poly(hexamethylene 2,3-O-isopropylidenetartarate) blend containing a photoacid generator (PAG, 2-(4-methoxystyryl)-4,6-bis(trichloromethyl)-1,3,5-triazine)). Upon UV irradiation, the PAG releases hydrochloric acid, which triggers the acid-catalyzed degradation of the PE component. This selective dissolution of one hemisphere not only increases the particle’s hydrophilicity but also creates channels for the ZVI to interact with contaminants. This dual-compartment strategy prevents ZVI agglomeration and ensures stable dispersion at non-aqueous phase liquid (NAPL)/water interface, resulting in enhanced transportability and efficient removal of both hydrophobic and hydrophilic pollutants.

The strategic design of the polymeric shell can also move beyond passive protection to active participation in the catalytic process through in-situ chemical modification. For instance, Wang et al. demonstrated this concept by developing QCS@Ag-TiO 2  core-shell microspheres, where the quaternized chitosan (QCS) core functions as a multifunctional template rather than a simple support (Fig.  9b ) 197 . A defining innovation of this study is the active dual-role of the biopolymer matrix. First, the positively charged QCS core acts like an “electrostatic magnet,” rapidly attracting and concentrating negatively charged pollutants from wastewater to the catalyst surface. Second, and most importantly, the QCS serves as an internal nitrogen reservoir during the synthesis of the shell. Through an in-situ doping process, nitrogen atoms from the chitosan are naturally incorporated into the titanium dioxide (TiO 2 ) lattice. This self-doping mechanism effectively narrows the bandgap, allowing the catalyst to be activated by visible light without needing external nitrogen sources. To further boost performance, silver (Ag) nanoparticles were added to generate localized heat (photothermal effect) and prevent energy loss. By combining the pollutant-concentrating ability of the core with the bio-engineered catalytic shell, this system achieved a remarkable 96.4% degradation of contaminants and complete inactivation of  E. coli . This approach exemplifies how biopolymers can be directly exploited to engineer high-performance catalytic platforms.

Moreover, the ultimate fate of the spent support material has become an equally critical consideration for true sustainability. Hao et al. addressed this by synthesizing g-C 3 N 4 /calcium alginate (SACN) hydrogel microspheres via a syringe dripping and cross-linking process for organic dye removal 198 . While the system achieved a high removal rate for RhB (Rhodamine B) through the synergy of adsorption and photodegradation, this study also conducted anaerobic biodegradation analysis. Under anaerobic conditions, the SACN microbeads underwent near-complete biodegradation within a 30-day period, successfully converting the spent support into a renewable methane feedstock. This approach ensures full-lifecycle neutrality by effectively repurposing a disposal liability into a sustainable energy feedstock.

The inherent functional versatility of biomolecule-based materials can also facilitate the stable immobilization of delicate biocatalysts under mild conditions. Liu et al. leveraged this advantage to develop a hierarchical chloroplast mimic using zinc/cystine (Cys(Zn)) microspheres 199 . The porous nature of this bio-inspired matrix allowed for the simultaneous encapsulation of photosensitizers, co-catalysts, and enzymes (ADH) without compromising their biological activity. This biomimetic system achieved a Turnover Number (TON) of 2112 for ADH by efficiently coupling photocatalytic and enzymatic pathways, maintaining stable performance for over 48 h. Integrating synergistic photocatalytic and enzymatic systems within a microsphere platform represents an innovative approach, offering a promising material design framework for sustainable green energy generation.

Despite the high performance of these biomimetic systems, the broad industrial adoption of biocatalysts is frequently hindered by the high cost of specialized matrices and co-factors. Recognizing these barriers, Zhou et al. developed a self-sufficient biocatalytic platform using chitin/chitosan composite microspheres (CCM) 200 . Their approach leveraged a simple hybridization of raw chitin and chitosan powders, in contrast to conventional supports that often require energy-intensive chemical modifications. By co-immobilizing both the enzyme and the expensive PLP co-factor within the CCM matrix, the need for continuous supplemenation of the co-factors was eliminated. While internal diffusion slightly reduced initial efficiency, the ability to maintain 83% activity over eight cycles effectively transforms a capital-intensive process into a mild, mass-producible industrial operation (Fig.  9c ). This work demonstrates that minimally processed biopolymers can bypass complex synthetic steps, offering a practical route toward the scalable and sustainable development of biocatalytic technologies.

Beyond their role as catalytic supports, polymeric microspheres, particularly those with core-shell architectures, are being investigated as encapsulation hosts for phase change materials (PCMs). PCMs store thermal energy as latent heat, providing a high energy storage density essential for applications such as building insulation, smart textiles, and thermal management in electronics. To address the environmental and biocompatibility concerns associated with petroleum-based shells, current research has shifted toward natural polymers including cellulose nanofibrils (CNF) 201 , chitosan 202 , and cellulose acetate 203 . However, the primary challenge lies in balancing sustainability with sufficient structural integrity to prevent leakage during phase transitions.

One of the sustainable synthesis strategies involves the use of CNF via Pickering emulsion stabilization, which avoids intensive chemical intervention. Kaya et al. demonstrated that this approach yields microcapsules with cyclic stability, retaining approximately 99% of their energy density after 200 cycles (Fig.  10a ) 201 . Despite these gains in sustainability, a significant structural limitation was observed. The reliance on self-assembly often results in a porous shell upon freeze-drying due to ice crystal sublimation, which can compromise long-term barrier performance. Similar porosity issues have been noted in shells fabricated via solvent evaporation or phase inversion. Watanabe et al. addressed this by implementing a shell densification strategy through polymer chain cross-linking 203 . By utilizing microfluidic flow processes to generate monodisperse droplets followed by PPG-TDI cross-linking, they achieved a dense, non-porous CA shell (Fig.  10b ). This structural refinement effectively eliminated the leakage issues inherent in simpler solvent-diffusion methods, allowing for a significantly higher latent heat capacity of 176 J/g. While optimizing the shell structure is vital for thermal efficiency, the integration of additional functionalities, such as magnetic separation, often introduces secondary thermodynamic costs. Chen et al. expanded the utility of PCM systems by incorporating magnetic Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles into a chitosan shell, enabling rapid magnetic recovery and recycling 202 . However, this multi-functionality comes at the cost of a notable enthalpy penalty, with thermal enthalpy dropping to a range of 73–80 J/g. This reduction is partly attributed to the presence of materials that do not contribute to latent heat, such as Fe₃O₄ and the the cross-linked polymer matrix, which delays heat transfer to the encapsulated alkane core. Alongside these structural and functional considerations, high-performance designs must also address kinetic barriers such as supercooling. While several studies have noted complex crystallization shifts under confinement, the incorporation of 1-hexadecanol as a nucleating agent has proven effective in facilitating heterogeneous nucleation, ensuring latent heat release at the precise phase transition onset 203 . Collectively, these advancements indicate that while natural polymers provide a viable path toward sustainable thermal energy storage, a universal, high-performance architecture has not yet been fully realized. Each fabrication strategy involves specific compromises, necessitating a prudent, case-by-case selection of materials and processes that balance thermodynamic efficiency with eco-friendly design. Harmonizing these demanding criteria remains a persistent challenge for researchers, requiring a commitment to green material selection without sacrificing the functional integrity essential for practical applications.

sections.heading: Other functional applications
paragraphs: Polymeric microbeads have been extensively utilized in several representative applications discussed in previous sections. Beyond these roles, they are also widely employed across a diverse range of fields, including coatings, construction materials, and optical property modulation for substrates 204 ,  205 – 206 . These industrial sectors possess broad application scopes and well-established global markets, where research into sustainable and eco-friendly alternatives is currently gaining significant momentum. Conventionally, microspheres incorporated into these sectors, particularly in coating resins, have been designed to tailor optical properties, strengthen mechanical performance, and impart functional traits such as superhydrophobicity or antibacterial activity. However, these systems have typically relied on non-degradable petroleum-based polymers, often overlooking long-term sustainability 207 ,  208 – 209 . To address these sustainability challenges, recent strategies have focused on incorporating functionalized microspheres into biodegradable polymer matrices to overcome their inherent limitations, such as flammability or lack of bioactivity, without compromising mechanical integrity.

For instance, in the field of sustainable construction and packaging, biodegradable polymers like poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT) are promising but suffer from high flammability. Zhang et al. demonstrated that incorporating phosphorous-silicon hybrid microbeads (SiP-M) into PBAT can significantly enhance fire safety 210 . Remarkably, a minute addition of 0.1 wt% SiP-M was sufficient to achieve a UL-94 V0 rating and a Limiting Oxygen Index of 26.5 vol%. These microbeads function through a synergistic mechanism: releasing phosphorus radicals in the gas phase to terminate combustion while promoting char formation in the condensed phase. Furthermore, by modifying the interface with a silane coupling agent, the incompatibility between the inorganic filler and organic matrix was resolved, ensuring that the tensile strength and elongation of the eco-friendly composite were maintained.

In tandem with these bulk material improvements, recent work has highlighted how eco-friendly spherical polymer particles can be engineered for advanced coating systems, combining sustainability with multifunctional performance 211 , 212 . For instance, PDA-based mesoporous microspheres have emerged as a versatile platform to replace fluorinated or toxic agents in advanced coating and surface-functionalized systems 213 , 214 . These microspheres enable the integration of self-healing and antifouling properties into resins, where surface roughness contributes to stable superhydrophobicity. A notable example is the development of P-PDMS@MPDA microspheres, created by loading polydimethylsiloxane into PDA carriers (Fig.  11a ) 214 . When incorporated into waterborne resins, these particles provide dual NIR- and pH-responsive release, allowing the coating to restore its superhydrophobic state and resist bacterial adhesion dynamically. Specifically, these functionalized microbeads serve as active reservoirs that are dispersed within a waterborne resin, which acts as the primary adhesive matrix. In this formulation, silica nanoparticles are added to the resin mixture to create the precise micro-scale surface roughness required for superhydrophobicity, and once the entire mixture is applied to a target substrate (such as metal or plastic), it solidifies into a functional composite film. This integrated design is vital for maintaining performance; because the delicate surface structures are highly susceptible to mechanical wear, the embedded microbeads autonomously release their encapsulated healing agents (e.g., PDMS or silicone oil) upon surface compromise to restore the coating’s water-repellent and anti-biofouling properties. Building on this concept, researchers have further evolved the internal architecture of these carriers from mesoporous matrices to hollow PDA shells containing an amino silicone oil core (Bio-OHMP) to significantly increase the loading of self-healing agents. By utilizing a hollow structure instead of a porous one, the beads can store a larger volume of functional oil, thereby extending the system’s durability 213 . Compared to the earlier system (P-PDMS@MPDA), these Bio-OHMP-based coatings maintained their superhydrophobicity for over 72 h even under harsh environmental conditions—effectively doubling the functional lifetime while showing enhanced responsiveness to multiple stimuli (Fig.  11 ).

Beyond industrial coatings and bulk composites, optical transparency is a critical requirement for next-generation green electronics, yet traditional biomass processing often suffers from thermal degradation before melting. Sun et al. overcame this by utilizing chitosan nanospheres (100 nm) to fabricate highly transparent thermoplastic films via a solvent-free hot-pressing method 215 . Unlike the original chitosan powder which degrades before melting, the high surface activity of the nanospheres allowed for molecular chain entanglement and fusion at lower temperatures (120 °C), which is well below the degradation threshold. The resulting films achieved an optical transmittance of 58% in the visible light range (400–800 nm), a significant improvement over the opaque films produced from untreated chitosan powder. This optical clarity, combined with respectable mechanical hardness (0.27 GPa), enabled the fabrication of biodegradable interdigital electrode substrates capable of sensitive capacitance measurements. This approach illustrates that precise morphological control of microspheres can unlock new optical functionalities in biomass materials, paving the way for fully green, transparent electronic substrates.

These advances demonstrate that microbead-integrated coatings are moving beyond simple passive protection toward active, multi-responsive platforms that offer both superior durability and sustainable multifunctionality. Nevertheless, the persistent reliance on petroleum-derived substances for the actual healing agents within these systems still poses a challenge for complete environmental sustainability, necessitating further investigation into fully green material alternatives 216 .

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: In summary, recent developments in eco-friendly microbeads and microspheres across the cosmetics, biomedical, environmental, and other sectors demonstrate clear and tangible progress toward sustainable polymeric materials that can replace petroleum-based plastics. Natural polymers offer biodegradability and safety, and recent advances in their functionalization and processing have significantly expanded their utility. Synthetic biodegradable polymers provide improved durability and scalability, whereas composite systems integrate the advantages of different materials to form multifunctional platforms with greater stability and broader application potential. Taken together, these advances highlight that the field is not only moving toward sustainability in principle but is already generating viable alternatives with real-world applications, including personal care products, targeted drug delivery, controlled release systems, water purification, and catalytic or energy-related technologies. As fabrication methods and material design strategies continue to mature, the design principles summarized in this review can guide the translation of laboratory-scale micro/nanosphere technologies into practical, sector-specific solutions that accelerate the transition away from persistent microplastics. However, important challenges still remain. Although biodegradable and naturally derived materials are often assumed to be eco-friendly, this is not always the case. Careful evaluation of processing impacts, durability, and degradation byproducts is essential to ensure true sustainability. Many promising results are still demonstrated only at the laboratory scale, and commercialization will depend on reproducible fabrication, cost efficiency, standardized evaluation frameworks, and regulatory alignment. In particular, the standardization of biodegradability testing is paramount. While most studies covered in this review were selected based on the assumption that bio-based or natural polymers possess inherent sustainability, it is noteworthy that a large number of these studies do not actually perform empirical biodegradability testing within their experimental results. Establishing unified evaluation protocols that accurately reflect real-world environmental triggers will be essential for providing transparent and reproducible data, which are currently lacking in many laboratory-scale studies. Furthermore, several critical research gaps remain that require closer attention. One major challenge involves the scalability of high-precision fabrication techniques, as current laboratory-scale methods often struggle with the throughput and cost-efficiency required to compete with conventional industrial processes. Another significant gap is the stability-degradability paradox, which describes the difficulty of maintaining structural integrity during a product’s shelf-life while facilitating rapid decomposition upon environmental release. This necessitates the development of stimuli-responsive systems that can be triggered by specific environmental factors. Moreover, long-term in-situ monitoring in diverse and complex ecosystems is required to assess the potential eco-toxicity of intermediate breakdown products. Addressing these complex challenges through cross-disciplinary approaches such as AI-driven material informatics will be key to ensuring that sustainable microbeads are not only biodegradable but also economically and functionally viable for global markets.

Moving forward, stronger partnerships between academia and industry, together with a greater focus on waste-derived feedstocks and multifunctional systems, will be critical. If these efforts continue, eco-friendly microbeads and microspheres can advance into scalable solutions that mitigate environmental burdens and establish themselves as practical, transformative technologies across a wide range of industrial applications.

sections.heading: Literature search methodology
paragraphs: This scoping review was conducted in strict adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines 217 , 218 . A comprehensive and systematic literature search was performed via Google Scholar to identify relevant studies across diverse industrial sectors, with the search restricted to peer-reviewed journal articles indexed in major academic databases such as Scopus or Web of Science. To ensure the inclusion of current research trends, only English-language articles published between 2015 and 2025 were considered, while theses, dissertations, conference proceedings, and patents were excluded. A primary search was conducted from July 20 to August 3, 2025, followed by a comprehensive two-stage update spanning from October 15 to November 30, 2025, and concluding between January 27 and February 1, 2026.

The scope of this review is specifically confined to spherical polymeric particles, encompassing microspheres, microbeads, microcapsules, and nanospheres derived from sustainable polymer matrices. Several exclusion criteria were applied to maintain a targeted focus; specifically, non-polymeric carbonaceous or metal materials were excluded unless utilized as fillers within a polymeric shell, and studies primarily evaluating the performance of scaffolds or bulk hydrogel systems were also omitted. The search strategy employed Boolean operators to integrate foundational keywords as follows: (eco-friendly OR sustainable OR biodegradable OR bio-based OR renewable OR biomass) AND (microsphere OR nanosphere* OR microcapsule* OR microbead* OR microparticle*). This initial query was further refined with additional keyword sets related to specific fabrication methods and industrial applications, including cosmetics, Janus microspheres, membrane emulsification, UV filters, and polymeric biosensors.

The selection process was conducted independently by two reviewers, with consensus reached through consultation with a third author to ensure the reliability of the included data. Records were screened based on their titles and abstracts to ensure they positioned sustainability or biocompatibility as a central design objective and demonstrated a clear, application-oriented focus. sections.heading: Classification of sustainable micro/nanospheres
paragraphs: Various fabrication methodologies have been developed for producing micro/nanospheres, including emulsion polymerization 219 ,  220 ,  221 – 222 , emulsion-based phase inversion 223 , spray drying 224 , 225 , electrospraying 226 , membrane emulsification 227 , coacervation 228 , and microfluidic techniques 52 . These processing routes play a critical role in determining key particle characteristics such as size distribution, morphology, porosity, and structural stability 229 ,  230 – 231 , and are comparatively summarized in Table  11  and Fig.  13 . In this review, sustainable micro/nanospheres are classified into three groups according to the composition of the resulting spheres: natural and biomass-derived polymers, biodegradable synthetic polymers, and composites (Fig.  14 ). The first group, natural and biomass-derived polymers, includes polymers existing in nature. These materials are well-known for their innate eco-friendliness and biocompatibility. This category includes polysaccharides (e.g., cellulose, starch, alginate, chitin/chitosan), which are widely used due to their abundance, ease of extraction, and versatile properties 232 . It also features proteins (e.g., gelatin, zein, silk fibroin) that offer unique advantages for biomedical applications by providing versatile surface chemistry and specific biological interactions 233 ,  234 – 235 . Furthermore, lignin, a complex polymer from plant cell walls, can provide antioxidant properties and UV protection 236 . Polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), a diverse group of microbially synthesized polyesters, are also included; they are notable for being fully bio-based and proven to be marine-biodegradable 237 . Finally, this category also covers other forms of biomass, such as materials extracted from agricultural residues and animal by-products. On the other hand, biodegradable synthetic polymers are those artificially synthesized through chemical polymerization, even when their monomers originate from renewable resources 238 . Prominent examples include PLA, derived from resources such as corn starch, and PLGA, a copolymer of lactic acid and glycolic acid. The degradation rate of PLGA can be precisely tuned by adjusting its monomer ratio 239 . While these materials are known to offer biodegradability and biocompatibility under physiological conditions, their degradation in natural soil or aquatic environments is markedly slower, often requiring several years for complete degradation, in stark contrast to the rapid 6-month timeframe typical of industrial composting 240 . For instance, PLGA with a 50:50 monomer ratio, which typically undergoes complete hydrolytic degradation within 50–60 days under physiological conditions (37 °C, pH 7.4), has been reported to exhibit less than 20% mass loss over a 6-month period in natural soil environments 240 , 241 . Fig. 13 Schematic of the fabrication methods mainly utilized for micro- and nanospheres, classified into physical and chemical processes. a  Emulsion-based phase inversion method: Solidification of polymer microspheres occurs through solvent diffusion or evaporation into a non-solvent medium.  b  Spray drying: Formation of solid particles by atomizing a liquid precursor into a heated drying medium enabling rapid solvent evaporation.  c  Microfluidics: Precise manipulation of fluids within sub-millimeter scale channels to generate highly monodisperse droplets within a continuous phase.  d  Membrane emulsification: Production of finely controlled emulsion droplets by injecting a dispersed phase (or pre-mixed emulsion) through a microporous membrane into a continuous phase, followed by solidification via solvent evaporation or diffusion.  e  Electrospraying: Generation of micro- or nanoscale droplets from a polymer solution using electrostatic forces under a high-voltage field.  f  Coacervation: A physicochemical process involving phase separation into polymer-rich and polymer-poor phases. It encompasses simple coacervation (driven by the changes in solvent or temperature) and complex coacervation (driven by the electrostatic interaction between two oppositely charged polymers).  g  Dispersion polymerization: A process where monomers, initiators, and stabilizers are initially solubilized in a homogeneous medium; as polymerization proceeds, the resulting insoluble polymer chains precipitate and form stable, dispersed particles.  h  Seed swelling polymerization: Particle growth achieved by the diffusion of monomers and solvents into pre-existing seed matrices, followed by polymerization within the swollen particles.  i  Emulsion polymerization: A process where polymerization is initiated within micelles, with monomers supplied by diffusion from droplets through the continuous phase, producing colloidal polymer particles.  j  Suspension polymerization: Monomer droplets suspended in an immiscible aqueous medium are polymerized under continuous mechanical agitation, with suspending agents providing steric hindrance and droplet stabilization. Hot air rapidly evaporates the solvent, drying the droplets into solid microspheres. • Operational simplicity • One-step particle formation • Scalable for industrial production • Narrow size distribution • High cost for equipment maintenance and operation • Product loss due to powder sticking to chamber walls • Risk of clogging and abrasion at the nozzle (optimization of various conditions required) 224 , 225 Microfluidic method Provides precise control of fluid flow. The liquid jet disintegrates into charged droplets which solidify upon solvent evaporation. • Can be operated at ambient conditions • Allows for complex structure (core-shell, hollow, cup, Janus, etc.) • Provides higher encapsulation efficiency, and prevents leakage or premature release of the core materials during fabrication • Use of organic solvent (dissolving polymer) may damage the bioactivity of biomolecules • Need for optimization for various parameters (needle gauge, solidification method, temperature, humidity, etc.) 226 Membrane emulsification The dispersed phase is forced through a porous membrane into the continuous phase, forming uniform droplets at the pore openings due to surface tension. • Cost-efficient and scalable • Produces uniform, predictable particle sizes • Mild conditions ideal for mechanical stress sensitive protein/peptide drugs • Risk of membrane contamination or fouling • Limited control over complex structures and precise size tuning compared to microfluidics or electrospraying 227 Coacervation Electrostatic interactions between oppositely charged polymers (triggered by medium changes, primarily pH or ionic strength) drive separation into a polymer-rich (coacervate) phase and a polymer-poor (equilibrium) phase. The coacervate phase forms droplets, encapsulating the core material. • Low cost and low energy • High loading efficiency via affinity partitioning • Utilize mild, often aqueous (solvent-free) processing conditions, which are favorable for protecting the bioactivity of encapsulated molecules • Easy agglomeration of microspheres after phase separation (disadvantageous for large-scale industrial production and storage) • Requires a post-processing step (e.g., cross-linking) for solidification • Process sensitivity; requires strict control over various parameters (e.g., pH, temperature, agitation) 228 Chemical Process Emulsion polymerization Monomer, water, emulsifier, and initiator are combined and polymerized. • Reliably yields microspheres with excellent monodispersity • Efficient, yielding high-molecular-weight products • Soapless method provides clean surfaces and eliminates emulsifier-related risks • Excessive use of emulsifiers can compromise microsphere performance • Difficulties involved with removing emulsifiers (restricting medical applications) • Difficult to control large or small size range, or embed functional substances 222 Suspension polymerization Monomer droplets containing an initiator are suspended in an immiscible liquid. The polymerization reaction then proceeds individually within each droplet, converting the liquid monomer into a solid, spherical polymer particle. • Low separation cost • Low dispersion viscosity compared to bulk polymerization • Easy heat removal and temperature control due to the aqueous medium • Difficult to control particle size distribution (requires precise regulation of stirring speed or dispersant usage to achieve monodispersity) • Polymer build-up (Reactor fouling), since polymer tends to stick to reactor walls and agitators 220 Dispersion polymerization Monomer, dispersant, initiator, additive and solvent form a homogeneous mixture. Growing polymer chains precipitate and aggregate, stabilized by dispersants and mechanical stirring. • Effective for monodispersed polymeric microspheres in a single batch • Integration with other methods (microwave/ultrasound) reduce reaction time • Polymerization process requires organic solvents which might be harmful and needs thorough purification and separation process 219 Seed swelling polymerization Small "seed" microspheres (from emulsion/dispersion polymerization) are swollen by inert solvent and monomer, followed by heat-induced polymerization. • Ideal for preparing micro-ranged monodisperse polymer microspheres • Enables precise control over microsphere size and pore distribution • Relies on swelling agents • Involves a complex reaction process, lengthy preparation, and relatively high costs (mostly done in two-steps and limiting scalability) 221

Their sustainability advantage is therefore most evident in controlled biomedical contexts rather than in broader environmental settings. Finally, composite systems are engineered by combining distinct components to achieve enhanced properties that are unattainable with individual components alone. In this review, composites are specifically defined as hybrids across primary classes, such as polymer-inorganic (e.g., alginate and silica) or natural-synthetic blends (e.g., alginate and PLGA). Note that mixtures of polymers within the same class (e.g., chitosan–alginate) are discussed under the “natural polymers” category in this review.

In addition to this material-based classification, this review summarizes how sustainable micro/nanospheres have been engineered and applied across key domains. These include cosmetics and personal care products, biomedical and pharmaceutical systems, environmental remediation and purification, and emerging industrial applications such as functional coatings, catalyst carriers, and energy storage platforms. The following sections survey these domains, highlighting representative examples and recent advances.

Monomer, dispersant, initiator, additive and solvent form a homogeneous mixture. Growing polymer chains precipitate and aggregate, stabilized by dispersants and mechanical stirring.
• Effective for monodispersed polymeric microspheres in a single batch • Integration with other methods (microwave/ultrasound) reduce reaction time
• Polymerization process requires organic solvents which might be harmful and needs thorough purification and separation process
Small "seed" microspheres (from emulsion/dispersion polymerization) are swollen by inert solvent and monomer, followed by heat-induced polymerization.
• Ideal for preparing micro-ranged monodisperse polymer microspheres • Enables precise control over microsphere size and pore distribution
• Relies on swelling agents • Involves a complex reaction process, lengthy preparation, and relatively high costs (mostly done in two-steps and limiting scalability)
